title: Finding V max and K M in a patient

segs.text: Module eight, objective three. Finding V max and K M in a patient. V max is the fastest the body can eliminate the drug, a rate in milligrams per day or milligrams per kilogram per day. K M reflects the capacity of the enzyme system. It is a concentration, so it can be compared directly with the drug level, and on the elimination curve it is the level at which the rate is half of V max. Both can be measured in test tubes, but a patient's own values come from that patient's steady state levels, and objective four uses them to choose the dose.

card.m: V<sub>max</sub>: the fastest elimination rate, mg/day or mg/kg/day
at C<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>M</sub>: rate = ½ V<sub>max</sub>

segs.text: The rate at which the body eliminates the drug equals V max times C p, divided by K M plus C p. When C p is much smaller than K M, C p hardly changes the bottom of the fraction, so the rate is V max over K M, times C p. The rate then rises in proportion to the level, which is first order. When C p is much larger than K M, K M hardly matters, the levels cancel, and the rate stays close to V max whatever the level. That is zero order.

card.m: example, C<sub>p</sub> 1 mg/L: {{frac:12 × 1|10 + 1}} = 1.09, close to 1.2 × 1: first order
example, C<sub>p</sub> 100 mg/L: {{frac:12 × 100|10 + 100}} = 10.9, close to 12: zero order

segs.text: At steady state the dose going in each day equals the drug eliminated each day. So the daily dose rate R equals the elimination rate at the steady state level, C s s: R equals V max times C s s, over K M plus C s s. Read along the curve, a higher dose rate needs a higher level before the body eliminates it all. Below K M the level rises in step with the dose. As the dose rate nears V max the curve flattens, so the level has to climb steeply, and a small change in dose gives a large change in concentration.

card.m: steady state: rate in = rate out
R near V<sub>max</sub>: a small rise in R, a large rise in C<sub>ss</sub>

segs.text: One measured level is not enough, because the line has two unknowns, V max and K M. So the patient gets two different dose rates, each held until its steady state is measured. For a drug like this, that takes two to three weeks, not three to five half lives. Both pairs come from the same patient, so they share one V max and one K M, and combining the two lines gives K M first. Each term in the K M line is a dose rate divided by its own level, so K M comes out in milligrams per liter.

card.m: pair 1: R<sub>1</sub> → C<sub>1</sub>   pair 2: R<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>

segs.text: Her slide example shows the effect. Six milligrams per kilogram per day gave a steady state of ten milligrams per liter. A linear drug keeps the level in proportion to the dose, so eight milligrams per kilogram per day would have given about thirteen. Instead, eight gave twenty: one third more dose doubled the level. The pair gives a K M of ten milligrams per liter, and either pair then gives a V max of twelve milligrams per kilogram per day.

Reading the results back against the curve ties them to the formula. At ten milligrams per liter the level equals K M, so the elimination rate is half of V max, six, the dose rate she gave. At twenty, the rate is eight, two thirds of V max. So the closer the daily dose comes to V max, the more steeply the level climbs. She said, I wrote this twice because you should get the same answer regardless of which way you use it.

The usual errors come from the same lines. K M is a concentration, so a rate unit on K M is wrong. Subtracting the ratios in the wrong order makes K M negative. And V max must use one pair's dose rate with that same pair's level, never one dose with the other dose's level. The seventy two kilogram weight is used only when a dose for this patient is asked, in objective four.

card.m: K<sub>M</sub> in mg/L, never a rate unit
V<sub>max</sub>: R and C<sub>ss</sub> from the same pair
